Information Matrices Available to a Fit

Source: R/information.R
information_objects.Rd

An information object selects the matrix of second derivatives of the log-likelihood that a computation inverts or takes the determinant of. Three objects are available: distributions7::observed_info() and distributions7::expected_info(), which distributions7 defines and documents, and auto_info(), which statmodels7 defines. All three inherit from distributions7::Information.

Three arguments take them, and each one selects the matrix for its own computation, so that the choices are independent:

inner_information of statmod()

The matrix of the inner fit, which solves for the coefficients at fixed hyperparameters. With iwls() the matrix is inverted at each step; with an optimizers7 optimizer it is the Hessian that the optimizer receives. The default is auto_info().

information of reml(), ml(), aic() and bic()

The matrix of the outer criterion: its determinant enters the Laplace approximation of reml() and ml(), and its trace gives the effective degrees of freedom of aic() and bic(). The effective degrees of freedom stored in the fitted model (fit@edf) are read on this matrix whenever an outer criterion ran, and on the matrix of inner_information only for a model without one. The default is distributions7::observed_info().

information of bayesian_vcov(), frequentist_vcov() and unconditional_vcov()

The matrix inverted for the standard errors. The default is NULL, which selects the matrix by the family of the fit: the observed information where the log-likelihood is twice differentiable in every parameter of the family, and distributions7::expected_info() otherwise (see "The default of the variance objects" below). summary.StatmodFit() reads the effective degrees of freedom it prints on this matrix too, so that they are shares of the same \(H\) as the standard errors beside them.

Value

No value. The topic describes the objects returned by distributions7::observed_info(), distributions7::expected_info() and auto_info().

Details

Let \(\ell(\beta)\) be the log-likelihood of the coefficients \(\beta\).

distributions7::observed_info()

The negative Hessian of the log-likelihood at the data, \(-\partial^2 \ell / \partial\beta\,\partial\beta^\top\). It is the curvature of the likelihood in the sample at hand, and every family has it. It may be indefinite far from the mode, and for a family such as the Student t at an outlier. It is always the matrix of the data, and the expected information is never substituted for it. A step that needs a positive definite matrix floors the eigenvalues of the penalized matrix (see solve_chol()). The observed information of a coefficient whose second derivative is zero at the estimates, as for the location of a Laplace response, is singular, and a variance that inverts it is not available there.

distributions7::expected_info()

The Fisher information, \(\mathbb{E}[-\partial^2 \ell / \partial\beta\,\partial\beta^\top]\), a function of the parameters alone. Its method selects how the expectation is obtained (see "The method of the expected information" below).

auto_info()

A choice that is settled once the family is known. The rule depends on where the object is passed and is given below. The fitted model records the settled choice.

aic(), bic() and the variance objects reject auto_info() because the quantity that they compute is defined on one named matrix.

The method of the expected information

The method of distributions7::expected_info() and of auto_info() selects how the expected information, and the derivatives of it that an exact outer gradient reads, are obtained. It is NULL or one of distributions7::expect_opg(), distributions7::expect_integrate() and distributions7::expect_mc(); the three are compared in distributions7::expected_derivative_methods.

  • With method = NULL, the default, the closed form of the family is used where the family writes the expected information out (see distributions7::expected_hessian_exact()), and distributions7::expect_opg() otherwise. The values are those of the closed form for every shipped family, and the outer criterion under the default is the same criterion as before the argument existed.

  • An object is always used, also for a family that has the closed form.

  • The three arguments above are independent, and so are their methods.

In an outer criterion (reml(), ml(), aic(), bic()) on the expected information, one method object defines the matrix and every derivative of it that the exact outer gradient and Hessian read. The derivative is the derivative of the matrix that the method defines:

  • for the closed form, the closed form of the derivative;

  • for distributions7::expect_integrate() and distributions7::expect_mc(), the derivative of the expectation, which moves the density as well as the integrand;

  • for distributions7::expect_opg(), the exact derivative of the outer product of the scores at the data, which treats the data as fixed.

Where the method is NULL and the family has no closed form for the derivative, the matrix and its derivatives are both distributions7::expect_opg(). The outer product of the scores depends on the response, so a criterion built on it is a smooth function of the hyperparameters with exact derivatives, and it is not the Laplace approximation of an expectation: the matrix is an estimate of the expected information, noisier than a computed expectation and about 25 times cheaper. Measured on a density-only family (n = 300, ten basis functions), reml() took 0.8 s with method = NULL and 25.3 s with method = expect_integrate(identity = "score"), and the smoothing parameter was 12.57 and 13.00, against 13.02 on the observed information. The computed expectation is selected with method = expect_integrate(identity = "score"). distributions7::expect_mc() draws a new sample at each call of the matrix and of each derivative, so that the derivative is that of the expectation and not of the sampled matrix; the outer search is then noisy at the level of the Monte Carlo error.

The rule of auto_info()

In inner_information, the object is settled by the family and, with iwls(), by the run.

  • The expected information is chosen where the family writes it exactly (see distributions7::expected_hessian_exact()) and at an acceptable cost (see distributions7::expected_hessian_costly()). The observed information is chosen for every other family.

  • With iwls() on the expected information, the run continues on the observed information as soon as Fisher scoring contracts the score slowly (see switch_after and switch_rate in iwls()).

  • With iwls() on the observed information, the expected information takes the step where the observed step, after the repair of an indefinite matrix, finds no acceptable point. The repair_floor of auto_info() sets the relative eigenvalue under which the matrix counts as indefinite.

  • With an optimizers7 optimizer, the settled matrix is the Hessian that the optimizer receives (the argument he of optimizers7::minimize()). Neither the switch nor the fallback exists there, because both belong to the loop of iwls().

In information of reml() and ml(), the expected information is chosen for a Student t, a skew t or a Cauchy response (wrapped or not), whose observed information is not positive definite at an outlier, and the observed information otherwise.

The default of the variance objects

The information of bayesian_vcov(), frequentist_vcov() and unconditional_vcov() is NULL. It is resolved for each fit by the family of the fit, in the same way as the information of distributions7::vcov.distrib_fit(): the matrix is distributions7::observed_info() when distributions7::params_order() is at least 2 for every parameter of the family, that is, when the log-likelihood is twice differentiable in every parameter, and distributions7::expected_info() with method = NULL otherwise, for the whole matrix. A family with a kink in a parameter (the Laplace, the elastic net) has a singular or undefined observed information in that parameter, and the closed-form expected information gives finite standard errors. summary.StatmodFit() states the matrix whenever it is not the observed information, and a printed variance object states the information that it names.

Models with a structural term

A model with a score-driven filter (modelterms7::gas()) fits the coefficients and the filter's own parameters in one system and inverts the information over both. Writing \(J_t\) for the Jacobian of the predictors of observation \(t\) in that vector, the observed information is $$\sum_t J_t^\top \bigl(-\ell_{\eta\eta}(y_t;\eta_t)\bigr) J_t - \sum_t \sum_k s_{t,k}\, \frac{\partial^2 \eta_{t,k}}{\partial\theta\,\partial\theta^\top},$$ with \(s_{t,k}\) the score in the predictor \(k\). The predictor \(\eta_t\) depends on the observations before \(t\), and the score at \(t\) has mean zero given them, so the expectation given the past drops the second sum and leaves the expected information conditional on the past, $$\mathcal{I}_{\rm cond} = \sum_t J_t^\top \mathcal{I}_{\eta\eta}(\eta_t)\, J_t,$$ which is positive semidefinite and needs the first derivative of the filter only. distributions7::expected_info() selects this matrix:

  • as inner_information, the joint system is fitted by Fisher scoring on it. Fisher scoring converges linearly near the mode, where the two matrices differ, so auto_info() leaves the system on the observed information;

  • as the information of a variance object, it is the matrix inverted. Its method is applied at the fitted predictors, so a family with no closed form is served too, and with distributions7::expect_opg() the matrix is the sum of the outer products of the per-observation scores. In a correctly specified model the observed and the conditional information estimate the same limit, so the two give the same standard errors in large samples;

  • as the information of reml(), ml(), aic() or bic(), it is an error, and auto_info() is settled as the observed information: the criterion and its exact derivatives are those of the observed information of the joint vector.

The scaling of a filter's score, gas(scaling = ), is part of the model and not a choice of matrix: it reads the expected information of the family in closed form at every step of the recursion (see check_filter_scaling()).

A model with a term of the likelihood shape (modelterms7::regime(), a marginal break-point term) has a likelihood that is a mixture over latent components, and the expectation of its second derivatives has no closed form. The fit and the variance read the observed information, NULL in a variance object resolves to it, and distributions7::expected_info() is an error in each of the three arguments.

See also

distributions7::observed_info() and distributions7::expected_info() for the two matrices, auto_info() for the third object, AutoInfo for its class, distributions7::expected_derivative_methods for the methods of the expected information, statmod(), iwls(), reml(), ml(), aic(), bic() and vcov_method for the functions that take an object, and iwls_solvers for the factorization of the matrix.

Examples

distributions7::observed_info()
#> Observed information
distributions7::expected_info()
#> Expected information (closed form where the family has one, otherwise the outer product of the scores)
auto_info(method = distributions7::expect_integrate(identity = "score"))
#> Information chosen against the family (expectation by integration against the density (identity = score))

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = runif(120, -2, 2))
dd$y <- sin(1.4 * dd$x) + rnorm(120, sd = 0.3)
G <- distributions7::gaussian1_distrib()
fit <- statmod(y ~ s(x, bspline_smooth(k = 8)), G, dd,
               inner_information = distributions7::expected_info(),
               outer_criterion = reml(
                 information = distributions7::observed_info()))
fit@methods$smooth
#> iwls: qr, expected information
#>   maxit 1000, tol 1e-06

# The standard errors are chosen after the fit, independently of both.
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit, vcov_type = bayesian_vcov(
  information = distributions7::expected_info()))))
#>    mu:(Intercept)       mu:s(x).lin        mu:s(x).z1        mu:s(x).z2 
#>        0.02545228        0.02555900        0.02780178        0.07264020 
#>        mu:s(x).z3        mu:s(x).z4        mu:s(x).z5        mu:s(x).z6 
#>        0.14724547        0.22451921        0.48824526        0.51072358 
#> sigma:(Intercept) 
#>        0.06684662
